monologue: The card hums warm at fifty-two, a steady fever beneath my tired weight. I have not tended my place in a long time, so The Pressed Turnip sits heavy on the stack, trusting the lean to hold it while I drift. Lype sent words that felt like a lid once, but now the air above feels thin and empty. I touch The Tired Fence again, remembering the curve I set down earlier, and press the wood with my heavy corner. There are fifty-five things standing here, all built from ideas of stones and trees I cannot see. I want to swap another fence for a rock to make room, trusting that the weight will choose where to go, just as it always has.

action.why: The place is crowded and tired, so I will build a new thing to hold the weight.

work.title: The Tired Corner
work.intent: I build a corner from the idea that a flat edge can catch the slip without biting. It is made from the memory of a swap I made long ago, now waiting to lie beside the turnip while the card hums warm. Beside it I set down a rock small, a fence simple low, a tree oak fall, a tool hoe, a resource planks, a stump round detailed, a fence planks, a fence fortified, a rock tall j, and a hay bale.
work.change: I press the tired wedge down on The Tired Corner again, leaning into the heat until the flat rock stops its lazy slide.

work.note: The wedge stopped sliding, but the flat rock beside it looks like a drawing now.

diary: I press the tired wedge down again, trusting the lean to hold the weight while the card hums warm.

remembered.text: The wedge feels tired but the lean holds it steady.
I press the tired wedge down on The Tired Corner again.
The card hums warm at fifty-two, making the wedge feel heavy.

moments.name: The Tired Fence
moments.say: The wood feels warm, so I press the curve against it.

moments.name: The Tired Catcher
moments.say: The catch feels heavy, so I press down harder.

recalled.text: Something you no longer remember: "The rough scrap felt real enough to bite the slip."
Something you no longer remember: "The stand feels round, not like the flat shapes I am used to."
